sections.title: Best Time for the Makalu Base Camp Trek
sections.html:
Best Time for the Makalu Base Camp Trek 

Autumn and spring are the best times to do the Makalu Base Camp Trek. Both of these seasons have their own special appeal and they stand out because of exceptional scenery. 

The Autumn season (September to November) is many trekkers' dreams. This post-monsoon season has clear skies and you will get to see crystal-clear views of Makalu and many other surrounding ranges. 

During autumn, the weather is stable. So, flights to Tumlingtar are more reliable. It is a peak season for exploration of the Himalayas of Nepal. 

Spring (March to May) is another ideal time for the Makalu Base Camp Trek. This month, the trails of the stunning Makalu region are filled with rhododendron blooms. In addition, many other Himalayan wildflowers can also be seen along the trail which enhances the sightseeing experience of the trekkers. 

During both the autumn and spring seasons, the likelihood of heavy downpour and snowfall is very low. So, the trails are dry which makes your navigation easier. The likelihood of weather related trip cancellations is also low at this time. So, you can ensure a smooth and timely conclusion of the adventure. 

Immersing in the stunning scenery is one of the major reasons that people join the trek and the spring and autumn season present an exceptional visibility which is considered perfect for sightseeing. So, for a smooth Makalu Base Camp Trek, trekking in these peak seasons is highly recommended. 

How to Train for the Makalu Base Camp Trek? 

Makalu Base Camp Trek is an adventurous journey and is rated as a moderate to challenging journey in terms of difficulty.During the trek, you will be stopping at varied high-altitude areas. So, you have to be well prepared for the trek. Generally, the experts recommend training for at least 3 to 4 months before trekking. 

When you are well prepared for the trek, you can navigate the varied terrains and have more endurance and strength. You may include strength and cardio exercises in your routine, as they will help you stay fit and have enough energy to tackle the trek difficulties. 

The strength exercises recommended for the Makalu Base Camp Trek are as follows: 

  • Planks
  • Step Ups
  • Deadlifts 
  • Push Up 
  • Squats 
  • Calf raises 
  • Lunges 

Many trekkers also choose to do cardio exercises. These are essential for a smooth adventure in the Himalayas. Some cardio exercises that are a must for the Makalu Base Camp trek are as follows: 

  • Swimming
  • Jogging or Running
  • Climbing the stairs 
  • Jumping Rope 

Another recommended training for trekkers is hiking. You may go hiking in your nearby hilly sections. This helps you be familiar with the actual trekking conditions, which will make your actual trek relatively easier and you will know what you can expect during the trek. 

Makalu Base Camp Trek Permits 

Makalu Region is gifted with stunning landscapes. However, the area is protected. So, to enter this area, a permit is essential. You have to obtain the following permits for the Makalu Base Camp Trek: 

  • Makalu Conservation Area Permit 
  • Makalu Rural Municipality Permit 

These two permits are a must for the Makalu Base Camp Trek. In addition, there are also some restricted parts in the region. If you decide to visit the villages like Hatiya, Chepuwa, Pawakhola and Kimathangka, you have to get a Restricted Area Permit. 

If you book your Makalu Base Camp Trek package with us here at Base Camp Adventure, we will obtain all the necessary permits so that you can enjoy the trekking adventure fully. 

What to Pack for the Makalu Base Camp Trek? 

Clothing 

  • Moisture-wicking t-shirts
  • Thermal base layers (top & bottom)
  • Fleece jacket 
  • Down jacket 
  • Waterproof jacket 
  • Waterproof pants
  • Trekking Pants & Shirts 
  • Insulated pants 
  • Quick drying undergarments 
  • Warm hats
  • Sun hats 
  • Buff
  • Windproof Jackets 
  • Neck gaiter
  • Gloves 

Footwear 

  • Trekking socks 
  • Woolen socks 
  • Sandals 
  • Trekking Boots 
  • Slippers 

Other Required Essentials 

  • Passport 
  • Nepal visa
  • Trekking Entry Permits 
  • Travel Insurance 
  • Backpack
  • Trekking Poles
  • Rain cover 
  • Dry bags
  • First Aid Box with essential medicines 
  • Route Map (Makalu Base Camp Trek Map) 
  • Water purification tablets
  • Thermos Bottle 
  • Toothbrush and Toothpaste 
  • Comb 
  • Flashlights 
  • Saftey Whistle 
  • Rain Gears 
  • Sanitizer
  • Tissues/ Wet Wipes 
  • Power Bank 
  • Headlamps 
  • Sleeping Bag 
  • Sunscreen
  • Lip balm 
  • Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) 
  • Cash
  • Mobile Phone 

About Altitude Sickness and the Acclimatization Process 

Altitude Sickness During the Makalu Base Camp Trek 

Trekking to Makalu Base Camp is a gratifying adventure through scenic Himalayan landscapes.  During the trek, you will make your way through rugged Himalayan terrain. However, as you climb higher, your body has to work harder because of lower oxygen levels. 

During this adventure, altitude sickness is a serious concern, especially if you have not acclimated. The trekkers generally began feeling the effects above 2,500 m However, symptoms can show up in even lower areas if your body is unable to adjust well. The common signs of altitude sickness are: 

  • Feeling tired 
  • Headache
  • Trouble falling asleep 
  • Dizziness
  • Appetite Loss 
  • Shortness of breath
  • Nausea and Vomiting 

Acclimatization 

While the likelihood of altitude sickness indeed exists during the Makalu Base Camp, with proper acclimatization and awareness, you can prevent and manage altitude sickness. Here are some ways to acclimatize properly on the trail. 

  • Ascend Slowly. Don’t rush at high altitudes. 
  • Stay Hydrated and eat nutrient-rich meals. 
  • Consider taking Diamox. This medication can help you acclimate faster. But talk about its use to your doctor before the trek to know if it's right for you. 
  • Follow the acclimatization schedule and take time to rest when needed. 
  • Head down to lower altitudes if you feel the symptoms and they do not get better. 

Guides and Porters 

The Makalu Base Camp Trek takes you to one of the most remote regions in Nepal. During this adventure, you will have to navigate a rugged and uneven landscape for almost 16 days.

This region is one of the most pristine areas and is visited by only a few trekkers. So, you have to be accompanied by someone who knows all about this area. Thus, trekking with a guide is essential. 

The expert guides are familiar with the Makalu region's terrain. Likewise, they can monitor your health and also respond quickly during emergencies. With their support, you can only focus on admiring the surrounding scenery while they help you with navigation and management of logistics. With their support you can ensure a secure adventure in the serene Makalu Region.

For this adventurous journey, porters also make a significant contribution. They carry your load and help you reduce the physical strain. This keeps you safe and allows you to focus on the trek without worrying about transporting luggage between stops. 

Porter will handle your baggage safely and make sure it gets to your stop on time. With their support, you can conserve energy and walk comfortably on the trail while fully enjoying the experience without getting distracted because of the heavy loads. 

The support of guides and porters is needed for trekkers' safety in a region with limited infrastructure. Along with the safety, they add cultural value to your journey. They share intriguing cultural facts and help you interact with locals making your overall adventure truly enriching. 

At Base Camp Adventure, we have expert guides and porters who will provide you with support and reliable insights that will make your adventure secure and reliable. 

Travel Insurance 

Trekking to Makalu Base Camp is thrilling. However, it takes you deep into remote part of eastern Nepal. The tough and remote terrain of the Makalu region requires you to have solid travel insurance. 

During this high altitude adventure, there is a risk of altitude sickness, injuries and sudden weather changes. Sometimes even emergency evacuation can be needed. Medical help is limited in this area. So, if something serious happens, you might need a helicopter rescue.

The helicopter evacuation can be incredibly expensive. In addition, while trekking you could face issues like losing your gear. Furthermore, flight delays, last-minute cancellations, or unexpected natural events, are also possible during this adventure. Without proper travel insurance, these unexpected events can be costly.

When picking a travel insurance plan for this trek, you need to be sure what it covers specifically. So, it is crucial to have protection for trip cancellations or lost baggage. 

Additionally, the insurance must also cover the medical bills incurred because of illness and injury during the trek. Most importantly, the coverage should include a helicopter rescue in emergencies. 

It is advisable to take time to carefully review the policy and purchase the one that provides coverage for high altitude trekking. By getting right insurance you can stay assured and trek with peace of mind knowing that you will be financially secure if unforeseen circumstances arise during the journey.  

Tips for a Secure and Joyful Makalu Base Camp Trek 

  • Research and inquire about Makalu Base Camp Trek cost, its highest altitude, and fitness requirements and then decide to join the adventure. 
  • Make checklist and pack all the required essentials for trekking.
  • Select the ideal seasons (Autumn and Spring) for a smoother adventure.
  • Always follow the instructions of your guide. 
  • Traverse only through the designated paths. 
  • Follow all the trekking regulations.
  • Focus on maintaining proper hydration and nutrition.

faqs.q: Where is Makalu Base Camp Situated?
faqs.a: Makalu Base Camp lies at an elevation of approximately 4,870 m. It lies within the Makalu Barun National Park which is located between Sankhuwasabha and Solukhumbu districts in Koshi Province, Eastern Nepal.

faqs.q: What is the Duration of the Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a:
The Makalu Base Camp Trek typically can be completed between 18 and 22 days. The exact time also depends on the chosen itinerary, acclimatization time and walking pace. 

At Base Camp Adventure, we have crafted a 16 day itinerary for the Makalu Base Camp trek, while making sure that you get to explore every scenic highlight of this awe inspiring and serene trekking route.

faqs.q: Why is Makalu Base Camp Trek Considered One of Nepal's Most Remote Treks in Nepal?
faqs.a:
Makalu Base Camp Trek is known to be among the remotest treks in Nepal. It involves navigating the remote villages, dense forests and rugged mountains. This region has limited infrastructure.

Situated in the Makalu Barun area this trek route sees few trekkers. So, it is an ideal choice for those who want to experience authentic Himalayas far from busy trek routes.

faqs.q: Is Guide Support Necessary for the Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a: Yes it is. Makalu Base Camp Trek is one of the most remote treks in Nepal. So support of expert guides who are familiar with the trails and challenges presented by trek is essential for smooth journey on the trail.

faqs.q: What is the Maximum Elevation of the Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a:
The highest altitude of the Makalu Base Camp is located at an altitude of about 4,870 m or which is the officially recognized altitude in all trekking routes. 

Certain extended routes and nearby ridges may reach elevations above 5,000 m but usually most trekkers trek up to 4,870 m at Makalu Base Camp.

faqs.q: Will Permits Be Checked at the Trekking Routes?
faqs.a: Yes. Permits will be checked. However, our guides will be there at the trail and will help you with the permit verification at different checkpoints, ensuring you a smooth and hassle free experience on the remote trails of Makalu.

faqs.q: How Difficult is the Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a:
Makalu Base Camp Trek is considered a demanding and strenuous journey that only fit trekkers can undertake. This trek can be completed in between 16 and 20 days. 

Along the trail, trekkers have to handle steep ascents and descents, rugged terrain and be well prepared to adjust to remote areas where facilities are limited.

faqs.q: Is Altitude Sickness A Risk on the Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a: Yes, it is. This trek takes you to remote high altitude regions where the oxygen level is low. At such high altitude areas, there is a likelihood of altitude sickness. That's why being attentive to signs and symptoms is necessary during Makalu Base Camp Trek.

faqs.q: How Can I Prevent Altitude Sickness During the Trek?
faqs.a:
To minimize the possibility of altitude sickness, you should walk slowly, drink plenty of water, have healthy food and avoid smoking and alcoholic beverages. In addition, make sure not to rush and follow the acclimatization schedule. 

Most importantly, you should never neglect the signs. If you are experiencing symptoms that are not getting better even after rest then head down to lower elevations. You may also bring medications for altitude sickness but please consult with your doctor for their safe use.

faqs.q: Is There A Scheduled Acclimatization Day During the Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a:
Yes. acclimatization day is scheduled during the Makalu Base Camp trek. Almost every well-crafted itinerary of the Makalu Base Camp trek has acclimatization days included in the package.  

At Base Camp Adventure, we have crafted the 16 days itinerary by including the acclimatization day in Langmale Kharka.

faqs.q: How Do I Get to the Trail Head of the Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a: To get to the start point of Makalu Base Camp, you will join the exciting flight from Kathmandu to Tumlingtar which takes about 35 minutes. Afterwards, you will enjoy a scenic road journey that takes you to Num, which is the main trailhead of the trek.

faqs.q: Where Does the Makalu Trek Begin and End?
faqs.a:
The trek to Makalu Base Camp usually starts on the eastern side of Nepal with Tumlingtar being the entry point for travelers, followed by a road trip up to Num, from where the trekking starts.  

After reaching the base camp of Makalu, trekkers walk along the varied path and make it to Num, drive to Tumlingtar and get back to Kathmandu on a flight.

faqs.q: Is it Possible to get a Customized Itinerary for the Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a:
Yes. You can get your Makalu Base Camp trek itinerary customized. If you make request to us then we can customize itinerary based on your available time, fitness level, schedule and your interest. 

By choosing customized itinerary you can enjoy a personalized experience on the trekking trails.

faqs.q: What Happens If Flights Between Kathmandu and Tumlingtar Are Delayed or Cancelled?
faqs.a:
In case of a delay or cancellation of your flight from Kathmandu to Tumlingtar there might be a need to make a change in your trekking schedule. 

We will help you arrange the next available flight as well as change the mode of transport and accommodations as necessary. Thats why we recommend you have a flexible schedule.

faqs.q: When is the Best Time for the Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a:
The best time to trek Makalu Base Camp is during the Spring and Autumn months. Both seasons provide stable weather, good visibility, mild temperatures and well defined trails offering a safe trekking environment. 

All these conditions make these season stand out as ideal for exploring the Makalu trails.

faqs.q: How are the Trail Conditions Like During Monsoon Season?
faqs.a:
During monsoon season, the region gets heavy rains. Paths could be muddy, slippery and difficult to navigate. The forested sections may have leeches and even landslides. Visibility is often poor because of the clouds.

Though the surroundings are lush green and clear weather presents distinct mountain views, the challenges should be considered before undertaking the journey. Trekking at this time is possible but not ideal.

faqs.q: What Weather Conditions Can Be Expected in Winter?
faqs.a:
The weather in winter for the Makalu Base Camp Trek is usually cold and very dry. The temperatures go way below zero, and there is usually snow in the higher passes. 

The sky is usually clear enough to enjoy the mountain views, but sometimes heavy snow, ice, and wind may lead to navigation problems. Also, handling the winter cold can be difficult for all. Thats why that season is usually not recommended and only experienced trekkers join the trek at this time.

faqs.q: What Accommodation Options are Available During the Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a:
The accommodation on the trekking route leading to Makalu Base Camp includes village guest houses, teahouses and very simple lodges. The lower sections mostly have well developed teahouses. 

The upper sections, near Makalu Base Camp, have very simple accommodations with limited facilities. Sometimes many trekkers also stay at tented camps. However, you will still get a good place to rest after a long day on the trekking trail.

faqs.q: What Foods Are Served on the Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a:
The food is generally basic, filling and nutritional, providing energy for trekking. The food menu includes dal bhat, fried rice, vegetable curry, Thukpa, noodles, pasta, chowmein, soup, potatoes, eggs, Tibetan bread, pancakes and momo. 

The beverage options include tea and coffee. With the increase in altitude of the trail, the menu items can be limited. However, fresh meals are still served on a daily basis.

faqs.q: Are Vegetarian and Vegan Meals Available?
faqs.a:
Vegetarian food is usually easily available on the trek. Some examples are dal bhat, vegetables and curries, potato dishes, rice, noodles, and soups.

If you want only vegan food, then please notify us so that we can make arrangements accordingly.

faqs.q: Is Safe Drinking Water Available on the Trail?
faqs.a:
Water can be found in teahouses, rivers, streams and other natural sources. However, raw and untreated water is not considered as safe for drinking. 

Trekkers can get boiled water at teahouses or purify the water from natural sources with purification tablets, and a UV purifier before drinking.

faqs.q: Can I Buy Snacks Along the Route?
faqs.a:
Snacks may be available at teahouses and shops in the lower villages. However, it becomes less available as you head further into the isolated areas. 

Finding your favorite energy bars, chocolate, nuts or other snacks along the way can be difficult along the trail. That's why we recommend you buy snacks of your choice prior to trekking.

faqs.q: Are Charging Facilities Available At the Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a:
Facilities for charging can be found at lower elevations, but electricity gets increasingly limited at higher elevations. Most teahouses provide charging facilities at extra cost. In some remote areas especially on the off beaten path, facilities for charging are limited.

So, we suggest you carry a power bank, extra batteries, and possibly even a solar charger. Make sure to keep your devices fully charged at lower elevations or whenever there is a chance.

faqs.q: Do Teahouses on Makalu Base Camp’s Trail Porvide Wi-Fi facilities?
faqs.a:
There is limited Wi-Fi availability at teahouses on the Makalu Base Camp trek. NTC and Ncell offer some coverage at lower elevations generally around the upper area villages. 

However, at higher camps, Wi-Fi services are quite slow and are provided at an additional cost.

faqs.q: Can I Rent or Buy Trekking Gear in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Yes you can. There are many stores in Kathmandu mainly in Thamel where you can buy or rent different trekking gear. You may either rent or buy trekking gear according to your preference. Just make sure to check quality of the gear for a comfortable experience on the Makalu trail.

faqs.q: What Clothing Should I Pack for the Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a: For the Makalu Base Camp trek we suggest you bring layered clothing (Base Layers, warm mid layers, and waterproof outer layers). In addition, you can bring a rain jacket, down jacket, trekking pants, thermal clothes, warm socks, gloves, hats and a warm beanie.

faqs.q: How Should I Train Physically for the Trek?
faqs.a:
It is necessary to prepare 3 to 4 months prior to joining the Makalu Base Camp journey by doing cardio and strength training workouts. Some examples of cardio workouts are cycling, swimming, climbing the stairs, running etc. Likewise, you can also hike to nearby higher sections to get used to walking and developing stamina. 

Similarly, many trekkers also recommend doing strength exercises such as deadlift, planks, squats, push-ups and step-ups. Training for the Makalu Base Camp trail beforehand helps you build the strength that is required to navigate the varied trails.

faqs.q: Is the Makalu Base Camp Trek Safe?
faqs.a:
While the Makalu Base Camp Trek is relatively safe for trekkers who are adequately prepared it is one of the most challenging and remote adventure in Nepal.

The high altitude, unpredictable weather conditions, difficult terrains, limited medical facilities are some of the major factors that can make trek challenging. But with proper preparation and support of guide you can tackle these challenges and complete the trek smoothly.

faqs.q: What Safety Precautions Should I Follow?
faqs.a:
To ensure safety  you should follow a gradual itinerary with proper acclimatization days. In addition, you should keep yourself hydrated. Also, make sure to watch out for any signs of altitude sickness.

It is also advisable to bring warm clothing, waterproof clothes, a first aid kit, water purification kits and essential medications. In case you feel uneasy at any moment make sure to notify the guide immediately.

faqs.q: Should I Get Travel Insurance for the Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a:
Yes. It is required. During the Makalu Base Camp Trek, you will be at remote high altitude locations where the facilities are limited. 

Like any other trekking adventure, there are certain risks involved, such as sudden accidents because of injuries, altitude sickness or interruption because of weather related issues. Sometimes helicopter evacuation may also be necessary. 

Without insurance, the cost of evacuation is quite high. Thats why it is essential to have travel insurance.

faqs.q: What Should the Travel Insurance for Makalu Base Camp Trek Cover?
faqs.a: Travel insurance for the Makalu Base Camp trek should cover up to the highest altitude in your itinerary. It must cover medical treatment, emergency helicopter rescue, trip delays and interruption, evacuation and loss of baggage.

faqs.q: What Happens In Case of an Emergency?
faqs.a:
In an emergency situation, your guide will analyze the situation and make decisions accordingly. If necessary, evacuation will be organized.

According to the situation, you might have to descend or get evacuated through a helicopter. 

The trekkers who need evacuation are mostly taken to Kathmandu or some other hospital for treatment.

faqs.q: Is Helicopter Evacuation Available?
faqs.a: Yes. It is possible especially in case of an emergency though factors like weather conditions, visibility and availability of helicopters can play a major role in availability. Guides will coordinate with us as well as the rescue team and arrange quick evacuation when necessary.

faqs.q: Can I Take Medicine for Altitude Sickness?
faqs.a:
Yes you can. Medications like as Diamox may help prevent or reduce risk. However, we suggest you to consult your doctor beforehand. But proper acclimatization remains essential throughout the trek. Thats why, you must follow the acclimatization guidelines.

If serious altitude sickness symptoms develop safest response is to stop trekking up further and head down to lower areas immediately.

faqs.q: How Do I Book Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a:
Booking the Makalu Base Camp Trek package with Base Camp Adventure is an easy process. You may visit out website and open the trek’s package page. Then, select the “Book This Trip” option.

Afterwards, you can choose the departure date. Then, specify the number of trekkers. You may then complete the required booking details and pay 30% advance for confirmation.

For additional information, you can contact us at 977-1-4517875 (landline) or +977 9851029616 via WhatsApp or Viber or through phone call.  You may also send an email to info@basecampadventure.com.

faqs.q: How Much Extra Money Should I Carry for the Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a:
We recommend carrying additional money up to US$ 250 to 350 (converted to Nepali rupees) on this trekking route. You may spend the money according to your personal spending habits.  

This can cover snacks, beverages, hot shower, charging, internet, souvenir purchases, and other expenses. As there are no ATMs in the remote places, you should withdraw money from Kathmandu.

faqs.q: Is Tipping Expected?
faqs.a:
Yes. It is. Though tipping is not compulsory it is widely practiced in Nepal. Guides and Porters make your adventure easy and achievable by providing the required support during the trek. 

They are always with you during this journey, looking after your well-being and health.  

The amount guides and porters receive in the form of tips can be a lot of help for their livelihood. In addition, they will feel appreciated for their hard work and be motivated to continue the exceptional service even for their future treks. So, tipping is the best way to appreciate their hard work.

faqs.q: How Much Tip is Recommended for the Makalu Base Camp Trek?
faqs.a:
The tipping amount for the Makalu Base Camp Trek is not fixed. There is no standard amount. It depends totally on your experience with the guides and porters' services on the trail.

To give you an idea trekkers usually pay around 10%-15% of the total trek cost as tips for the trekking team. However, you may tip any amount you wish.

overview:
Manang is one the most beautiful hidden valley of South Asia- which can be conquered in a Manang Trek. It is a Nepalese village which is approximately 250 km from the national capital Kathmandu.

It is far from the capital but no one can feel that it is in far remote distance. This is because the available facilities can match the one of Shangri-La. Manang (3,540 m) is one of the largest villages in Manang district and one of the last trekking stops for trekkers walking the famous Annapurna Circuit trek.

From Manang the route continues to Thorung La (pass) at 5,415 m above the sea level which connects Manang district to Mustang District by providing a route between the town of Manang and the village Muktinath. This part of trail of Manang trek to Muktinath has been used by the locals for hundreds of years to transport huge herds of sheep and yak in and out of Manang.

The northern part of town is more preserved in its old style; in the southern part you will find many hotels, shops and even a cybercafe, with satellite internet connection.

Manangies are well-known traders and many of them are relatively rich having property in both Manang and Kathmandu and their children study in good schools or even abroad.

Many trekkers spend one acclimatization day in Manang or surroundings although the surroundings are interesting enough to stay for several days.

The 9 days of  Manang Trek features several interesting spots, including the glacier lake at the base of the icefall on the slopes of Gangapurna Mountain, the village of Braga, Bhojo Gompa, Milarepa Cave, and Ice Lake. There are several options to extend your trek by two or three day side trip to Tilicho Lake the highest-altitude lake in the world or the most demanding Thorang-la pass trek which will make your adventure even more unforgettable.

itinerary.title: Arrive at Kathmandu airport and transfer to hotel.
itinerary.html: Arrive at Kathmandu, you will be  picked by our representative who will then transfer you to hotel. Overnight in Kathmandu.

itinerary.title: Private Jeep drive from Kathmandu to Jagat (1,300 m / 4,265 ft), 7-8 hours
itinerary.html: Today our journey begeins with the scenic jeep driving along the highway to Beshisahar which is the main gate way of Manang Trek, Annapurna Circuit Trek or Tilicho Lake Trek. From there we continue our drive through Marsshyangdi River valley to Jagat . Overnight in Jagat.

itinerary.title: Trek start from Jagat to Bagarchhap (2,160 m / 7,087 ft), 5-6 hours
itinerary.html: From here we commence our trek with continuing to ascend alongside Marsyangdi River, we cross a waterfall before Chamje and then pass through spectacular fields and lush rhododendron forests on our way to Bagarchhap. We cross many suspension bridges and climb steeply on twisted trails with the view of Annapurna II (7,937 m) and Lamjung Himal (6,983 m) emerging in the backdrop. Crossing the villages of Tal, Karte, and Dharapani, we arrive in Bagarchhap. Overnight in Bagarchhap.

itinerary.title: Trek from Bagarchhap to Chame (2,670 m / 8,760 ft), 6-7 hours.
itinerary.html: From Bagarchhap we continue to climb through pine and oak forests, pass through Danakyu, and ascend up to Timang village which lies at the bottom of Lamjung Himal (6,983 m). Often rough and rocky, the track climbs to Thanchowk and then continues through the forest to reach Koto. A gradual stroll alongside Marsayangdi River takes us to Chame, the headquarters of Manang district. Amazing views of Lamjung Himal (6,983 m) and Annapurna II (7,937 m) are seen from Chame. Overnight in Chame.

itinerary.title: Trek from Chame to Pisang (3,200 m / 10,499 ft), 6-7 hours.
itinerary.html: Today's trek starts with the deep forest in a steep and narrow valley and then crosses Marsayangdi River on a long bridge. We then cross another bridge before continuing to trek through the pine and cypress forest to reach Bhratang. Then we trek uphill to reach Dhikur Pokhari, from where we follow the gradual trail leading to Pisang. In Pisang, we’re surrounded by the Annapurna range on one side and Pisang Peak (6,091 m) on the other. Enjoy the amazing overnight stay in Pisang.

itinerary.title: Trek from Pisang to Manang (3,540 m / 11,614 ft). 8-9 hours
itinerary.html: There is two option to follow the way to Manang village. Although a little steep, the upper trail via Nawal to Manang is blessed with breathtaking views of the mountains as well as the verdant hills in the front. As we walk past the settlements of Ghyaru, Ngawal, Munchi, and Braga, we come across many small monasteries, including the 900 years old Braka Gompa. A short climb from Braka Gompa takes us to the beautiful village of Manang, situated between Chulu Himal range and the Annapurna range. Overnight in Manang.

itinerary.title: Explore Manang village (3,540 m / 11,614 ft) and its surrounding areas on an optional sightseeing excursion
itinerary.html: We spend the entire day exploring Manang and its outskirts. We hike to the beautiful Gangapurna Lake for a closer view of the Annapurna range and Gangapurna Peak (7,454 m). We also explore the old Manang vicinity which is known as Tengi. We then visit the ancient monasteries around Manang and also interact with the friendly locals. Overnight in Manang.

itinerary.title: Private Jeep drive from Manang to Kathmandu, 10-11 hours
itinerary.html: Today we head back from Manang to Kathmandu. The jeep will arrive in Mamang the night before we leave to Kathmandu. The trail follows Marsayangdi River downstream, and passing a few meadows and bushes of juniper, we gradually descend until reaching to Beshisahar with amazing views of the Annapurna massif dominate the landscape en-route.  Overnight in Kathmandu.

gallery.alt: How difficult is the Manaslu Trek

overview:
The Manaslu Circuit Trek is a 13-day guided journey around Mount Manaslu, the world’s eighth-highest mountain at 8,163 m (26,781 feet). The route follows the Budhi Gandaki Valley, crosses Larkya La Pass at 5,106 m (16,752 feet), and descends into the Annapurna region.

Starting with a drive from Kathmandu to Machha Khola, the trail passes through Jagat, Deng, Namrung, Samagaun, Samdo and Dharamsala. After crossing Larkya La, you descend through Bimthang and finish the trek at Dharapani.

Along the way, you will walk through river valleys, forests, alpine landscapes and traditional villages influenced by Tibetan Buddhist culture. There are numerous suspension bridges, waterfalls, monasteries, mani walls, and mountain views on the way that add variety to each day.

An acclimatization day in Samagaun helps your body adjust to the altitude. After that, depending on the weather and your fitness, you can hike towards Birendra Lake, Pungyen Gompa or Manaslu Base Camp.

Crossing Larkya La is the hardest part of the trek. It requires an early start and several hours of walking over steep, rocky, and sometimes snowy ground. You should be fit enough to walk for five to eight hours on consecutive days. Previous trekking experience is helpful, but a well-prepared beginner can complete the route with proper training and a guide to support & encourage them.

Manaslu is a restricted trekking area, so foreign travelers must obtain the required permits through a registered Nepali trekking agency and travel with a licensed guide. Independent trekking is not allowed, although solo travelers can book a private trip or join a group.

If you are looking for a quieter and more remote alternative to the Everest Base Camp or Annapurna Circuit, the Manaslu Circuit trek is ideal for you.

Manaslu Circuit Trek Route Map

The Manaslu Circuit Trek begins at Machha Khola, follows the Budhi Gandaki Valley, crosses Larkya La Pass, and ends at Dharapani. The complete route is:

Kathmandu → Machha Khola → Jagat → Deng → Namrung → Samagaun → Samdo → Dharamsala → Larkya La Pass → Bimthang → Dharapani → Besisahar → Kathmandu.

After driving from Kathmandu to Machha Khola, the trail follows the Budhi Gandaki River through cultivated hillsides, waterfalls, forests, and rocky gorges. Beyond Jagat and Deng, it enters the upper Nubri Valley, passing Tibetan-influenced villages such as Namrung, Lho and Shyala before reaching Samagaun.

Trekkers spend an extra night in Samagaun at approximately 3,530 m (11,581 feet) to acclimatize. The route then continues through Samdo and Dharamsala before crossing Larkya La at 5,106 m (16,752 feet). This is the highest and most demanding section, with snow, wind, and cold temperatures adding to the difficulty.

After the pass, the trail descends through Bimthang and continues to Dharapani, where the walking route ends. Ground transportation then connects Dharapani with Besisahar and Kathmandu. The detailed daily route, elevations, walking times, and overnight locations are explained in the itinerary below.

If you want a visual overview, you can also view the Manaslu Circuit trek map.

Manaslu Circuit Trek Altitude Chart
highlights: Cross Larkya La Pass at 5,106 meters (16,752 feet), the highest point of the trek.
See Mount Manaslu at 8,163 meters (26,781 feet) and surrounding peaks when visibility is clear.
Follow the Budhi Gandaki River through narrow gorges, forests, cultivated hillsides, and alpine terrain.
Cross numerous suspension bridges above rivers and waterfalls.
Walk through settlements including Jagat, Deng, Namrung, Lho, Shyala, Samagaun and Samdo.
Spend an acclimatization day in Samagaun, one of the principal villages of the upper Nubri Valley.
Take an optional acclimatization hike towards Birendra Lake, Pungyen Gompa or Manaslu Base Camp, depending on fitness and trail conditions.
Pass Buddhist monasteries, chortens, mani walls and prayer wheels that reflect the region’s Tibetan Buddhist heritage.
Travel through both the Manaslu Conservation Area and the Annapurna Conservation Area.
Experience a gradual transition from lower river valleys to high alpine and glacial landscapes.
Descend from Larkya La towards Bimthang, with mountain and glacier views in suitable weather.
Stay in locally operated teahouses and experience the practical rhythm of village-to-village trekking.
Complete the route with a licensed local guide who manages permits, pacing, accommodation, and trail decisions.

itinerary.title: Arrive at Tribhuvan International Airport (TIA), Kathmandu (1,400 m / 4,600 ft) and Transfer to Hotel
itinerary.html:
Your Manaslu Circuit Trek begins when you arrive at Tribhuvan International Airport (TIA) in Kathmandu. One of our representatives will meet you at the airport and take you to your hotel.
Once you have checked in, you can rest after your flight or spend some time exploring the nearby streets of Kathmandu. If you’re not tired, we recommend taking a stroll around the locality.

Overnight: Kathmandu

itinerary.title: Drive from Kathmandu to Machha Khola (863 m / 2,831 ft), 6-7 hours.
itinerary.html:
Fun fact: “Khola” means River in Nepali. You’ll hear it quite often in Nepal, as it has more than 6,000 “khola”s!

You leave Kathmandu early in the morning and drive towards Machha Khola. The journey takes around 6 to 7 hours, following rough and dusty roads through green hills, rice fields, waterfalls, and rural villages. But depending on the road conditions and weather, it may take longer.

Along the way, you pass Arkhet Bazaar (“Bazaar” means market in Nepali), an old local market beside Arkhet Khola. Slate-roofed houses, small settlements and changing countryside views keep the drive interesting until you reach Machha Khola, a small village surrounded by green hills.

itinerary.title: Trek from Machha Khola to Jagat (1,340 m / 4,396 ft), 6-7 hours.
itinerary.html:
On the third day, we begin walking along the narrow trail between the Budhi Gandaki River and the surrounding cliffs. The path leads towards Tatopani (“tato” means warm, “pani” means water; named due to the region’s abundant underground hot water sources) before continuing to Dobhan, Shyaule Bhatti, and Yaru.

Near Yaru, the Budhi Gandaki descends through a series of fast-moving cascades. After another 2-3 hours of walking, you arrive in Jagat, a stone-built village known for its slate-paved streets. Basic lodges and a campsite are available in the lower part of the village.

For people living in Jagat, tourism, agriculture, education, and government services are the main income sources.

itinerary.title: Trek from Jagat to Deng (1,860 m / 6,102 ft), 6-7 hours.
itinerary.html:
Leaving Jagat, you follow the riverbed and climb over a rocky section to reach Salleri. From here, you can see Shringi Himal rising to 7,187 m.

The trail continues along the left bank of the Budhi Gandaki River and climbs towards Philim. From Philim, you follow the track leading north towards Larkya La through thick forest and a narrowing valley.

After reaching Ekle Bhatti, the route crosses high above a deep gorge lined with pine trees. A gradual climb above the Budhi Gandaki Gorge then brings you to Deng for the night.

itinerary.title: Trek from Deng to Namrung (2,630 m / 8,629 ft), 6-7 hours.
itinerary.html:
The day begins by crossing the Budhi Gandaki River on a suspension bridge. You then climb through Rana and Bihi before following a trail that moves in and out of several gorges.

After crossing the Serang Khola, the path climbs sharply and circles into Ghap. The village has long mani walls carved with images of Buddhas in meditation, offering an early look at the Tibetan Buddhist influence found throughout the upper Manaslu region.

From Ghap, you enter a peaceful fir forest filled with birds like the Himalayan Monal, Blood Pheasant, Rufous Sibia, Streaked Laughingthrush, Green-backed Tit, and many species of woodpeckers. The trail crosses a wooden bridge beside a narrow canyon and continues uphill for around one and a half hours before reaching Namrung.

Note: “Mani” walls are stone walls built on either side of paths and near monasteries in the Himalayas, especially Nepal, Tibet, and Bhutan.

itinerary.title: Trek from Namrung to Samagaun (3,530 m / 11,581 ft), 7-8 hours.
itinerary.html:
Today’s trail passes through Bhanzam, where barley fields and traditional stone houses spread across the hillside. At the entrance to Lihi, you are welcomed by a panoramic mountain view that includes Manaslu at 8,163 m

After crossing Hinang Khola, you reach Lho. A large “gompa” (solitary Tibetan Buddhist monastery/compound where monks live, pray, teach, and learn) stands on the hillside above the village and provides a clear view of Mount Manaslu.

From Lho, the path climbs through forest towards Shyala, a compact village of closely arranged stone and wooden houses. You then cross the slope below Punggen Glacier and walk through open land where yaks graze before reaching Samagaun. The village sits beside a small river, with houses arranged in neat rows and the Manaslu mountain range rising behind them.

itinerary.title: Rest and Acclimatization Day in Samagaun (3,530 m / 11,581 ft), 6-7 hours.
itinerary.html:
On the 1-week mark of the journey, there is no need to rush because it is a rest day. The extra day in Samagaun gives your body time to adjust to the altitude before you continue towards Samdo, Dharamsala and Larkya La Pass.

You can rest in the village or join an acclimatization hike to Birendra Tal, Manaslu Base Camp, Pema Chyoling Lhakang or Punggen Gompa. Your guide will help choose a suitable option based on the weather, trail conditions and how you are feeling.

Whichever option you choose, you will spend another night beneath the Manaslu mountain in Samagaun.

itinerary.title: Trek from Sama Gaun to Samdo (3,875 m / 12,713 ft), 4-5 hours.
itinerary.html:
The trail climbs gradually from Samagaun, with Birendra Tal at 3,450 m resting below the Manaslu Glacier. You continue through open yak pastures lined with long mani walls.

Marmots are often seen standing near their burrows in this section. The path then climbs to a ridge before descending to a wooden bridge over the Budhi Gandaki River.

A final climb leads to a white chorten above the trail. Samdo lies just beyond it. The village depends heavily on yak herding, and you will notice that animal shelters and hay stores occupy much of the settlement.

itinerary.title: Trek from Samdo to Dharamsala (4,460 m / 14,633 ft), 4-5 hours.
itinerary.html:
You leave Samdo on a wide descending trail and cross the smaller upper section of the Budhi Gandaki River. The route towards Tibet branches off to the right, while you turn left and climb past a mani wall.

The trail continues through juniper bushes where marmots can often be spotted. After crossing two gorges along narrow paths, you reach Dharamsala, also known as Larke Phedi.

Dharamsala is a basic high-altitude stop with limited accommodation. Its stone building contains only a few rooms, but the surrounding area provides an open view of the Manaslu Himal Range (“Himal” means a mountain in Nepali). Rest well because the Larkya La crossing begins early the following morning.

itinerary.title: Trek from Dharamsala Across Larkya La Pass (5,160 m / 16,929 ft) to Bimthang (3,590 m / 11,778 ft), 8-9 hours.
itinerary.html:
This is the trek's main highlight and the longest, most demanding day of the Manaslu Circuit Trek. You start early and gain altitude slowly, following the large moraine beside the Larkya Glacier.

The ascent continues over rocky terrain and passes 4 frozen lakes. A final climb brings you to Larkya La Pass at 5,106 m, marked by prayer flags. When the weather is clear, the pass opens to wide views of the Manaslu Himal Range and Annapurna Range.

After spending some time at the pass, you begin the long descent along the western moraine. The trail remains steep in places before becoming gentler as you approach Bimthang.

itinerary.title: Trek from Bimthang to Dharapani (1,860 m / 6,102 ft) 7-8 hours.
itinerary.html:
The landscape changes noticeably as you leave Bimthang. The exposed mountain terrain gives way to greener surroundings, with the trail crossing below the Bimthang Glacier.

A short climb leads to an open area decorated with prayer flags. From here, mountains rise in several directions, while the Manaslu remains visible towards the southeast.

The route then enters a dense fir forest and continues to a solitary house at Yak Kharka, where you can stop for lunch. From Yak Kharka, you walk through more forest, pass Goa, and continue towards Dharapani, where the trekking section ends.

itinerary.title: Jeep drive from Dharapani to Besisahar, followed by a bus journey from Besisahar to Kathmandu, 8-9 hours.
itinerary.html:
You begin the day with an off-road jeep journey from Dharapani to Besisahar. The road descends towards Syange Village, climbs to Gharmu Phant, and then drops again towards Besisahar.

The jeep ride takes around 2-3 hours. After reaching Besisahar, you transfer to a tourist bus for the 5-to-6-hour drive back to Kathmandu.

It is a long travel day, but the route passes through hills, river valleys, rural settlements, and changing countryside. Once you arrive in Kathmandu, you will be taken to your hotel for the night.

itinerary.title: Transfer to Tribhuvan International Airport for your onward flight.
itinerary.html: Your Manaslu Circuit Trek comes to an end today. After breakfast, our representative will pick you up from your hotel and take you to Tribhuvan International Airport about 3 hours before your scheduled international flight.

sections.title: How Difficult is the Manaslu Circuit Trek?
sections.html:
The Manaslu Circuit Trek is a moderately challenging high-altitude trek. You do not need technical climbing skills, but you do need good fitness, proper preparation, and enough stamina to walk for several days in a row.

Most days involve 5 to 8 hours of walking over steep climbs, long descents, stone steps, suspension bridges, rocky paths, and uneven ground. The most demanding day is the journey from Dharamsala to Bimthang across Larkya La Pass. It begins before sunrise and can take 8 to 10 hours or longer when snow, ice, or poor weather affects the trail.

Altitude adds to the challenge. The route climbs from Machha Khola at approximately 870 m (2,854 feet) to Larkya La at 5,106 m (16,752 feet). With less oxygen available at higher elevations, even an ordinary walking pace can feel tiring. The pass crossing also takes you through cold, exposed terrain with few places to rest or shelter.

Under normal conditions, the trail does not require ropes, crampons or mountaineering experience. However, snow and ice around Larkya La can make microspikes useful. Strong winds, freezing temperatures and the long descent towards Bimthang can also make the day physically demanding.

Previous high-altitude trekking experience helps, but it is not compulsory. A well-prepared beginner can complete the Manaslu Circuit with structured training, proper acclimatization and realistic expectations. If you have not trained for long-distance walks or consecutive hiking days, you are likely to find the trek difficult.

Age alone does not decide whether someone can complete the route. Fit and experienced seniors often manage it well, while younger travelers can struggle when they arrive unprepared. Families should consider each person’s fitness, hiking experience, comfort with basic accommodation, and response to altitude before booking.

How to make Manaslu Circuit Trek less difficult?

You can reduce physical strain during the trek by:

  • Training for a few weeks before arriving in Nepal
  • Walking at a steady and comfortable pace
  • Using the Samagaun acclimatization day properly
  • Drinking enough safe water
  • Eating sufficient meals, even when altitude reduces your appetite
  • Carrying only essential items in your daypack
  • Reporting headaches, nausea or unusual tiredness immediately
  • Following your guide’s decisions about the weather, altitude and Larkya La Pass conditions

What Fitness and Training are required for Manaslu Circuit Trek?

You need good cardiovascular endurance, strong legs and enough stamina to walk for several days in a row. Begin training around 8 to 12 weeks before departure, so you improve gradually without putting too much strain on your body.

Start with brisk walking, hiking, cycling, swimming, or stair climbing. As your endurance improves, slowly increase the length of each session. This will prepare you for longer trekking days while reducing the risk of injury from doing too much too soon.

Alongside cardiovascular training, you should focus on strengthening your legs and core with squats, lunges, step-ups, calf raises and core exercises. Strong muscles around your knees and ankles will help you stay steady on steep climbs, long descents, stone steps and uneven ground.

Outdoor hill walking will prepare you most closely for the actual trail. Choose routes with climbs, descents, loose stones and steps whenever possible. Longer weekend hikes will also help you find a comfortable walking pace and identify problems with your boots, socks or trekking equipment before you travel to Nepal.

Once you feel comfortable on longer walks, carry the daypack you plan to use during the trek. Begin with a light load, then add water, extra clothing, snacks, personal items and safety essentials. You only need to train with the weight you expect to carry in Nepal.

You should also practice hiking on two or more consecutive days. One long walk can test your endurance, but walking the next morning again with tired legs reflects the demands of the Manaslu Circuit Trek even better. These back-to-back hiking days will help your body recover and continue walking throughout the journey.

Physical fitness is only part of the preparation. Accommodation becomes more basic at higher elevations, the weather can change quickly, and some walking days may take longer than expected. Being patient, adjusting your pace, and following your guide’s safety decisions will help you deal with these conditions.

If you have a heart, lung, joint, or other medical condition, consult a qualified medical professional before planning a high-altitude trek.

Recommended Preparation:

  • Walk or hike three to five times per week.
  • Complete a longer hill walk at weekends.
  • Practice climbing stairs and walking uphill for extended periods.
  • Add cycling, swimming or jogging to improve your endurance.
  • Strengthen your legs, knees, ankles and core.
  • Train in broken-in trekking boots.
  • Carry a loaded daypack during longer walks.
  • Walk on two or more consecutive days.
  • Gradually increase your distance, elevation gain and pack weight.
  • Include stretching, mobility exercises and enough recovery time.
  • Test your trekking poles, socks and clothing before traveling.
  • Reduce your training intensity during the final week before departure.

Training cannot predict how your body will respond to high altitude. However, arriving with good endurance and strength will help you walk more comfortably, recover between trekking days, and give your body the time and energy it needs to acclimatize.

Is the Manaslu Circuit Trek Safe?

You can complete the Manaslu Circuit Trek safely with proper acclimatization, physical preparation, suitable equipment, and an experienced licensed guide. But you must take the risks of altitude, changing weather, rough trails, and the remote location seriously.

Much of the trail lies several hours away from reliable road access. On top of that, mobile coverage is inconsistent, medical facilities are limited, and bad weather can delay both ground transport and helicopter evacuation. Because of this, you should prepare for the Manaslu Circuit as a remote, high-altitude trek, not an ordinary hike.

What are the main safety risks during the Manaslu Circuit Trek?

Here are the main safety risks:

  • Acute mountain sickness and other altitude-related illnesses
  • Snow and ice around Larkya La Pass
  • Sudden changes in temperature, wind, and visibility
  • Slippery trails near waterfalls and river crossings
  • Landslide-prone sections
  • Long walking days and physical exhaustion
  • Limited communication in remote areas
  • Delayed road transport or helicopter evacuation
  • Basic medical facilities along the route

Your guide will control the walking pace, monitor how you are feeling and change the daily plan when necessary. You also need to report symptoms honestly, follow safety instructions and speak up before a minor problem becomes more serious.

No guide, itinerary, or piece of equipment can remove every risk in the Himalayas. Your safety depends on careful decisions based on your physical condition, altitude, weather and current trail conditions.

How Does the Itinerary Support Acclimatization?

The itinerary helps your body acclimatize through a gradual ascent, a steady walking pace, and two consecutive nights in Samagaun before you continue above 3,500 m.

You begin trekking from Machha Khola at an altitude of 870 m and gain elevation over several days. This gradual climb gives your body more time to adjust than traveling directly to a high-altitude settlement.

Samagaun is the main acclimatization stop. You spend two nights there at approximately 3,530 m before continuing towards Samdo and Dharamsala. During the extra day, your guide may take you towards Birendra Lake, Pungyen Gompa or Manaslu Base Camp. The route will depend on how you feel, the weather, snow conditions, and the available time.

The aim is to walk to a higher elevation during the day and return to Samagaun to sleep. This follows the common acclimatization approach of climbing higher and sleeping lower.

You can acclimatize more comfortably by:

  • Walking at a slow and steady pace
  • Taking regular rest and hydration breaks
  • Avoiding unnecessary physical effort after reaching the teahouse
  • Eating enough, even when your appetite decreases
  • Paying attention to your sleep, energy, and physical condition
  • Reporting headaches, nausea or unusual tiredness early
  • Shortening the acclimatization hike if you feel unwell
  • Resting longer or descending when your guide considers it necessary

The itinerary includes one dedicated acclimatization day, but everyone responds to altitude differently. You may need an extra rest day or a slower itinerary. Do not shorten the route simply to save time if it requires you to gain altitude too quickly.

What is Acute Mountain Sickness?

Acute mountain sickness, or AMS, can develop when you ascend faster than your body can adjust to lower oxygen levels. It is a genuine concern on the Manaslu Circuit because the route reaches 5,106 m at Larkya La Pass.

Here are the warning symptoms:

  • Headache
  • Nausea
  • Dizziness
  • Unusual tiredness
  • Reduced appetite
  • Difficulty sleeping
  • Shortness of breath beyond what you would expect while walking
  • Poor balance or difficulty walking normally
  • Confusion or unusual behaviour

Do not ignore or hide even a mild symptom. You may feel tempted to remain silent because you do not want to delay the group or miss the Larkya La crossing, but hiding your condition can make it more serious when you don’t receive proper treatment and rest. If rest does not help or serious warning signs appear, you may need to descend to a lower elevation. Reaching Larkya La or following the planned itinerary must never come before your health.

Tell your guide immediately if you develop a headache, nausea, dizziness, or unusual exhaustion. Your guide can monitor your condition and decide whether you need to walk more slowly, rest, change the itinerary, or descend.

Your age, fitness, and previous trekking experience cannot predict exactly how you will respond to altitude. Even a strong and experienced hiker can develop AMS. Physical training will help you cope with the walking, but it will not protect you from altitude sickness.

What Does the Guide Monitor?

Your guide monitors your physical condition, walking pace, and response to altitude throughout the Manaslu Circuit Trek. Weather, snow, trail conditions and the progress of the entire group also influence each day’s decisions.

The guide pays attention to:

  • Headaches, nausea, dizziness and unusual tiredness
  • Your breathing and level of effort while walking
  • Balance, coordination and changes in behaviour
  • Your usual walking pace
  • Hydration and urine output
  • Appetite and ability to eat
  • Sleep quality
  • Recovery after reaching the teahouse
  • Oxygen saturation as a supporting measurement
  • Daily altitude gain
  • Weather forecasts and changes in visibility
  • Snow, ice and wind around Larkya La Pass
  • Trail damage, landslides and river conditions
  • Gaps between group members and the group’s overall progress
  • Whether you need rest, descent or an itinerary change

Your guide may use a pulse oximeter to check your oxygen saturation and heart rate. However, one reading cannot confirm that you are safe or unwell. The result must be considered alongside your symptoms, behaviour, altitude and overall condition.

Before crossing Larkya La, your guide will assess everyone at Dharamsala and check the latest weather and trail information. Heavy snow, strong wind, poor visibility or a health concern may require additional rest, a delayed departure, an itinerary change or a retreat.

How Are Weather and Trail Conditions Managed?

Your guide checks the weather and trail conditions throughout the trek, paying particular attention to the Larkya La crossing. Available forecasts, local teahouse owners, and reports from other trekking teams all help the guide decide whether it is safe to continue.

Conditions can change quickly at high altitude. A clear morning can turn into cloud, snowfall, strong wind, or poor visibility later in the day. For this reason, trekkers normally begin that day before sunrise.

Snow and ice can hide route markers around Larkya La and make the descent towards Bimthang slippery. Depending on the season and current conditions, your guide may recommend microspikes and trekking poles or change the departure time.

Rain, landslides, damaged bridges and trail repairs can also affect the lower route. During the monsoon, swollen rivers and unstable slopes require extra care. Your guide may stop the group, follow an alternative trail or wait for local confirmation before crossing a dangerous section.

Your itinerary may need to change when the planned route is unsafe. These decisions are made to protect you, so keep some flexibility in your international flight and accommodation arrangements.

What Happens During an Emergency?

During an emergency, your guide will assess your condition and take the safest immediate action available. This may include providing first aid, stopping the ascent, moving you to a sheltered place, or helping you descend to a lower elevation.

If further support is needed, your guide will contact the Base Camp Adventure office in Kathmandu. Our team can coordinate with local services, arrange available transportation, and communicate with your insurance provider.

An emergency response may involve:

  1. Stopping the group and assessing your condition
  2. Providing appropriate first aid
  3. Preventing you from ascending further
  4. Helping you descend when required
  5. Contacting our Kathmandu operations team
  6. Coordinating with teahouses, health posts or transport providers
  7. Informing your insurance assistance company
  8. Requesting helicopter evacuation when medically necessary and possible
  9. Transferring you to an appropriate medical facility

A helicopter evacuation cannot always take place immediately. Flights depend on the weather, visibility, daylight, landing conditions, aircraft availability, and approval from your insurer or assistance provider. If flying is not possible, you may need to descend on foot or use local ground transport until an evacuation can be arranged.

You must have travel insurance that covers trekking up to at least 5,106 m, emergency medical treatment, and helicopter evacuation in Nepal. Standard travel insurance can exclude activities above a certain altitude, so check the altitude limit and policy exclusions before departure.

Carry printed and digital copies of your insurance certificate, policy number, and emergency-assistance contact details. Base Camp Adventure can help coordinate an evacuation, but you and your insurer remain responsible for coverage approval and all related costs.

What Permits Are Required for the Manaslu Circuit Trek?

Foreign travelers need 4 trekking documents for the standard Manaslu Circuit route:

  1. Manaslu Restricted Area Permit
  2. Manaslu Conservation Area Permit
  3. Annapurna Conservation Area Permit
  4. TIMS card

These must be arranged before entering the controlled or protected areas.

Base Camp Adventure processes the required permits using your passport, tourist visa, confirmed itinerary, and personal details. You must carry the issued documents throughout the journey because they are checked at several points along the route.

1. Manaslu Restricted Area Permit

The Manaslu Restricted Area Permit, often shortened to Manaslu RAP, is required for the controlled section of the route in Chumnubri Rural Municipality. It is issued by Nepal’s Department of Immigration through a registered trekking agency.

The current official permit fees are:

Travel period

Fee for the first seven days

Additional fee

September to November

USD 100 per person

USD 15 per person for each additional day

December to August

USD 75 per person

USD 10 per person for each additional day

The amount depends on the number of days covered by the restricted-area permit, not the complete length of your holiday in Nepal. For this itinerary, the agency calculates the required validity according to the planned entry and exit dates.

The Department of Immigration can revise restricted-area boundaries, fees, and application procedures. Base Camp Adventure therefore reconfirms the applicable amount when processing the booking. Current rates can also be checked on the Department of Immigration’s official trekking-permit page.

2. Manaslu Conservation Area Permit

A Manaslu Conservation Area Permit (MCAP) is required from the point where the trek enters the Manaslu Conservation Area.

Current entry fees are:

  • Foreign nationals: NPR 3,000 per person
  • SAARC nationals: NPR 1,000 per person
  • Nepali nationals: NPR 100 per person
  • Children below 10 years: Free entry

The permit fee supports conservation management, environmental protection, and visitor infrastructure within the Manaslu Conservation Area. Jagat serves as the principal entrance to the protected area.

3. Annapurna Conservation Area Permit

An Annapurna Conservation Area Permit, or ACAP, is also required because the route enters the Annapurna Conservation Area after crossing Larkya La and descending towards Dharapani.

Current ACAP fees are:

  • Foreign nationals: NPR 3,000 per person
  • SAARC nationals: NPR 1,000 per person
  • Nepali nationals: NPR 100 per person
  • Children below 10 years: Free entry

Although only the final section of this itinerary passes through the Annapurna Conservation Area, the permit remains compulsory. Current MCAP and ACAP rates are listed by the Nepal Tourism Board.

4. TIMS Card

A Trekkers’ Information Management System card, known as a TIMS card, records the trekker, guide, agency, and planned route. Nepal Tourism Board’s current guidance lists the Manaslu Circuit among the routes requiring an agency-issued TIMS card and a licensed trekking guide.

Current TIMS charges are:

  • Non-SAARC nationals: NPR 2,000 per person
  • SAARC nationals: NPR 1,000 per person

Trekking agencies complete the online registration and generate an electronic card containing a QR code. Travelers cannot independently issue the agency-based TIMS card for this route. The latest requirements are available on the Nepal Tourism Board TIMS page.

Can You Trek the Manaslu Circuit Without a Guide?

No, foreign travelers cannot legally trek the Manaslu Circuit independently without a licensed guide because it is a restricted area. A solo traveler can still book the Manaslu Circuit as a private trip or ask to join a scheduled group departure. Traveling alone does not remove the agency, guide, or permit requirements.

All trekkers must remain on the approved route and follow the submitted itinerary. A side trip into another restricted area, such as Tsum Valley, requires an additional permit and an itinerary prepared for that route.

What Documents Are Needed for the Permits?

Travelers normally need to provide:

  • A clear colour copy of the passport information page
  • A copy of a valid Nepal tourist visa
  • A recent passport-style photograph
  • Full name, nationality, date of birth, and passport details
  • Arrival and departure information
  • Confirmed trekking dates
  • Emergency contact details
  • Travel-insurance information
  • A signed booking or trekking agreement, where required

Your Nepal tourist visa must remain valid throughout the trek. Permit information should also match your passport exactly, including the spelling of your full name, passport number, and nationality.

The Department of Immigration also requires the trekking agency to submit its registration documents, planned itinerary, guarantee letter, and insurance details for the accompanying Nepali staff.

Where Are the Permits Checked?

Permits are checked when entering or leaving the controlled and conservation areas at Jagat and Dharapani checkpoints. Additional verification is possible elsewhere along the circuit trail, so you should always keep your passport and permits with you.

Permits are issued to a named traveler for a defined route and period, and cannot be transferred to another person. If the itinerary changes significantly, the agency may extend or amend the permit.

Are Permit Fees Included in the Package?

Trekking packages you see online usually include permit fees, but it is always best to confirm with the agency before paying the booking deposit. At Base Camp Adventure, the necessary Manaslu trekking permits are arranged as part of the USD 1,130 per adult trek package. 

What is the Best Time for the Manaslu Circuit Trek?

The best times for the Manaslu Circuit Trek are spring (March to May) and autumn (late September to November). These seasons offer stable weather, less extreme temperatures, clearer mountain views, and the best trail conditions.

October and November are the most popular months. March, April and May are also suitable, although snow can remain around Larkya La early in spring. Winter and monsoon treks are possible only with greater flexibility and preparation because snow, rain, landslides, and transport delays can affect the route.
